Q60761435.summary: The Mother of God sits on a lavishly carved, high-backed throne with bolster cushions, holding the Christ Child upright on her lap, while two angels hover above with hands raised. The Child blesses with one hand and holds a scroll in the other, a solemn, ageless figure rather than an ordinary infant. An inscription runs along the base of the footstool, and the frontal, majestic composition belongs to a long Byzantine tradition of the enthroned Virgin and Child.
facts: The Cleveland Museum of Art dates the plaque to 950–1025 and attributes it to Constantinople.
It is called the 'Stroganoff Ivory' after its former owner, the Russian statesman and art historian Sergei Grigoryevich Stroganoff.
The museum notes that representations of the enthroned Virgin and Child in Byzantine art reach back as far as the 6th century.
Q60761435.notes: CMA 1925.1293; 25.3 × 17.2 cm. The Greek inscription on the base was not transcribed here.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-123-chris.summary: Blessed by the Hand of God, the bearded, cross-nimbed Christ-Logos stands at the head of the faithful — 'if it had not been the Lord who was on our side' — while below their enemies pursue others through a stream: 'then the waters had overwhelmed us'. Three who have escaped climb toward Christ past a fowler whose snares the birds have slipped. It is the lower drawing of folio 72v.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
Its text is written in rustic capitals, an archaic script that once led scholars to date the manuscript to the 6th century; the drawings are now recognised as Carolingian.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-123-chris.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server. This folio carries two drawings; the crop shows the one for this text.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-145-chris.summary: The cross-nimbed Christ-Logos holding a bannered cross-staff sits in a globe-mandorla among six angels, while the psalmist points a hungry crowd to a table of food, urging them to trust God rather than princes. An angel heals the blind and crippled; below, two princes enthroned order executions, and widows and orphans raise their hands to heaven. It is the upper drawing of folio 81v, 'Put not your trust in princes'.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
The psalter was made in or near Reims, probably under Archbishop Ebbo (816–835); some scholars argue for a date around 850 under his successor Hincmar.

cur:manuscripts2-otto-iii-peters-mother-.summary: Within a pedimented temple frame, the upper register shows Christ stretching his hand toward Peter's mother-in-law, who sits up on her bed while apostles watch. Below, small black devils fly out of the possessed as the crowds bring their sick to him, and onlookers raise their hands in wonder.
facts: The Gospels of Otto III has 276 leaves, twelve canon tables, a double-page portrait of the emperor, four evangelist portraits and 29 full-page miniatures of New Testament scenes; it was produced at Reichenau around 1000.
The Bayerische Staatsbibliothek has published the whole manuscript online with a Public Domain Mark, so every page can be studied in detail.
cur:manuscripts2-otto-iii-peters-mother-.notes: Folio derived from the BSB image sequence (image 302); verify against the foliation on the page.
